To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the molecular chaperones HSP90 and HSP70 do not accumulate in chloroplasts under mild HP.
the heat‐accumulated proteome in moss does not contain HSP chaperone proteins, but rather a large number of signalling proteins, which may contribute to the onset of AT.
the molecular mechanisms of AT in Physcomitrium are different from the well‐known mechanisms of heat shock response (HSR) and are not based on the accumulation of HSP chaperons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of plant thermotolerance and the role of molecular chaperones in the acquisition of heat tolerance.
the role of heat priming in AT and how this is accomplished by a specific set of proteins.
the molecular mechanisms of plant acquired thermoresistance, and the data provides the basis for future research into the function of the heat‐accumulated protein pool.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HP‐induced HSPs are not required to prevent protein aggregation, but rather to prevent cell death.
the role of HSP20s in AT is still an open question.
HP‐induced accumulation of HSP20s in the cytosolic proteome is a prerequisite for AT in moss, but that their role in preventing protein aggregation is not supported by the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the molecular chaperones that are thought to prevent protein aggregation in the chloroplast are not required to establish AT, whereas the cytosolic HSP20s that are not thought to be involved in preventing protein aggregation, are required.
HP induces AT through a mechanism that is not based on HSPs preventing protein aggregation, but on HSPs regulating the activity of rare proteins.
the molecular mechanisms that lead to AT in P. patens are not based on protein stabilization by HSP chaperone networks, but rather on the modulation of specific signalling pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular mechanisms of AT are not only different from heat shock responses, but also from the classical heat stress response, where HSPs are the main players.
the role of HSPs in AT is not to protect proteins, but to protect cells from dying by modulating the activity of key signalling proteins.
the molecular chaperones that are central to AT in the model moss P. patens, are not the HSPs.
